title: Stoma Perfusion: Color Tells You About Tissue Viability
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: A healthy stoma is expected to be moist and perfused. Dusky, purple, black, unusually pale, or progressively deteriorating tissue can indicate ischemia and requires prompt surgical escalation.
recognize: Normal postoperative swelling can occur, but worsening discoloration or loss of viable appearance is not routine.
priorities: Inspect color, moisture, edema, bleeding with gentle contact, and output trend; escalate suspected ischemia promptly.
assessMonitor: Trend stoma appearance, output, abdominal pain/distention, vital signs, and surrounding skin.
interventions: Avoid constricting the stoma with an undersized pouch opening or tight appliance.
medicationSafety: Do not use vasoconstrictive topical products on the stoma unless specifically ordered.
teaching: Teach patients to know their normal stoma color and seek urgent help for darkening or severe change.
delegationScope: Routine pouch care may be shared according to policy; ischemia recognition and escalation require licensed nursing judgment.
examTrap: Calling a blackening stoma 'normal postoperative bruising.'
oneLinePearl: Darkening stoma tissue is perfusion failure until proven otherwise.

title: High-Output Ileostomy: Dehydration Can Develop Quickly
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: A substantial increase in ileostomy output can cause rapid fluid, sodium, and renal losses. Dizziness, thirst, oliguria, tachycardia, weakness, or rising creatinine requires prompt escalation.
recognize: Watery output plus reduced intake, infection, medication change, or early postoperative state increases dehydration risk.
priorities: Measure output accurately, assess hydration/perfusion, and report clinically significant increases or dehydration cues.
assessMonitor: Track ostomy volume/character, intake, urine output, daily weight, BP/HR, renal function/electrolytes as ordered.
interventions: Reinforce prescribed fluid/electrolyte plan and obtain timely medical review for persistent high output.
medicationSafety: Antimotility agents or electrolyte replacement require individualized orders; do not self-treat severe output without review.
teaching: Patients should know their usual output pattern and when to contact the ostomy/surgical team.
delegationScope: Output measurement may be delegated; interpretation and escalation require licensed judgment.
examTrap: Focusing on the pouch while missing falling urine output.
oneLinePearl: High ileostomy output threatens kidneys as much as the pouch seal.

title: Peristomal Skin Injury: Effluent Should Not Sit on Skin
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Peristomal skin should remain intact. Burning, denudation, weeping, fungal changes, or repeated leakage usually signals appliance fit, moisture, mechanical injury, or skin-disease problems that need correction.
recognize: Liquid effluent and repeated adhesive trauma can rapidly damage skin and worsen pouch adhesion.
priorities: Identify the leakage/fit cause rather than repeatedly adding tape over a failing seal.
assessMonitor: Inspect skin pattern, stoma size/shape, pouch opening, creases, output consistency, and adhesive removal technique.
interventions: Use gentle cleansing and appropriate barrier/pouching technique; involve wound/ostomy specialists for persistent injury.
medicationSafety: Topical antifungal or steroid products should match the diagnosed skin problem and not impair pouch adhesion.
teaching: Teach gentle pouch removal and avoiding harsh products that damage skin or impair adhesion.
delegationScope: Routine pouch care may be assigned to trained staff; persistent skin breakdown requires licensed evaluation.
examTrap: Treating leakage by making the pouch opening larger.
oneLinePearl: Protect skin by fixing the seal, not by covering the burn.

title: Ostomy Obstruction: No Output Plus Cramping Is Not Reassuring
bottomLine: A sudden decrease or absence of expected ostomy output with cramping, distention, nausea, vomiting, or swollen stoma can indicate obstruction. Escalate rather than assuming the pouch is simply empty.
recognize: Partial obstruction may cause thin liquid output before output stops completely.
priorities: Assess abdominal/stoma findings and hydration, stop inappropriate oral intake if ordered/clinically necessary, and notify the surgical team.
assessMonitor: Trend output, pain, distention, vomiting, stoma edema/color, urine output, and vital signs.
interventions: Follow surgical/ostomy instructions; do not insert objects or irrigate unless specifically ordered and appropriate to ostomy type.
medicationSafety: Avoid reflexive laxatives or antidiarrheals until obstruction is evaluated.
teaching: Report abrupt output cessation with pain or vomiting promptly.
delegationScope: Output observation may be delegated; obstruction recognition/escalation requires licensed judgment.
examTrap: Giving a laxative because output has stopped.
oneLinePearl: No output plus symptoms means obstruction until proven otherwise.

title: Stoma Prolapse or Retraction: Fit, Perfusion, and Function Matter
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: A protruding or retracted stoma can compromise pouch fit, drainage, and sometimes perfusion. New major shape change, pain, obstruction, or color change requires specialist/surgical review.
recognize: Retraction increases leakage risk; prolapse can swell and become difficult to pouch.
priorities: Assess stoma color/perfusion, output, pain, appliance fit, and whether the change is new/progressive.
assessMonitor: Trend length/position changes, edema, output, leakage, and surrounding skin.
interventions: Protect the stoma from trauma and obtain ostomy/surgical guidance for appliance adjustments.
medicationSafety: No medication corrects a mechanical stoma complication by itself.
teaching: Teach patients to report new major protrusion, sinking, darkening, or loss of output.
delegationScope: Routine observations may be shared; mechanical complication assessment/escalation requires licensed judgment.
examTrap: Forcing a prolapsed stoma back in without an order/qualified assessment.
oneLinePearl: Shape change becomes urgent when perfusion or output changes.

title: JP and Hemovac Drains: Suction Only Works When the System Works
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Closed-suction drains require intact tubing, secure connections, correct reservoir compression, and accurate output measurement. Sudden output changes can indicate clogging, bleeding, dislodgement, or a change in the underlying wound.
recognize: Loss of suction, tubing kinks, leakage, abrupt high bloody output, or sudden stop in expected drainage are abnormal cues.
priorities: Inspect the entire system and surgical site before simply re-compressing the reservoir.
assessMonitor: Trend amount/color/character, suction status, insertion site, pain, swelling, and vital signs.
interventions: Empty/measure/re-establish suction according to the device and facility protocol.
medicationSafety: Do not instill medications or flush a surgical drain unless specifically ordered for that drain.
teaching: Home patients should secure tubing, record output, and know when to call the surgical team.
delegationScope: Routine emptying may be assigned to trained staff depending on policy; abnormal output requires licensed review.
examTrap: Documenting zero output as improvement without checking for obstruction.
oneLinePearl: A quiet drain can be empty—or blocked.

title: Nephrostomy Drainage: Protect Flow and Watch for Infection
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Nephrostomy drainage must remain unobstructed and secured. Reduced output, flank pain, leakage, fever, bloody change, or tube displacement can signal obstruction, infection, bleeding, or loss of access.
recognize: Kinked tubing, a bag positioned above the kidney, sediment, or dislodgement can reduce drainage.
priorities: Inspect tubing/bag position and insertion site, compare output trend, and escalate symptomatic changes promptly.
assessMonitor: Trend urine volume/color, flank pain, temperature, site drainage, tube position/securement, and renal function as ordered.
interventions: Maintain dependent drainage and follow exact flushing instructions only if prescribed.
medicationSafety: Do not irrigate or instill medication into a nephrostomy without a specific order/protocol.
teaching: Keep the bag below kidney level, avoid pulling, and report fever, pain, or sudden output loss.
delegationScope: Routine output recording may be delegated; troubleshooting and escalation require licensed judgment.
examTrap: Flushing a silent nephrostomy automatically before checking the order and tube position.
oneLinePearl: No nephrostomy output plus symptoms needs evaluation, not improvisation.

title: Biliary Drain Safety: Flow, Color, and Position Tell the Story
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Biliary drains require secure positioning and prescribed drainage/capping instructions. Fever, RUQ pain, jaundice, leakage, reduced output, or dislodgement can indicate obstruction, cholangitis, or loss of access.
recognize: Abrupt drainage change plus worsening jaundice or pain is more concerning than an isolated color change.
priorities: Check tubing position/securement, output trend, symptoms, and prescribed external-drain/capping plan.
assessMonitor: Trend bile amount/character, temperature, RUQ pain, jaundice, insertion site, and hydration.
interventions: Maintain prescribed drainage and contact the procedural team for blockage/dislodgement concerns.
medicationSafety: Do not flush or cap/un-cap outside the prescribed plan.
teaching: Teach patients the exact drainage/capping plan and urgent symptoms.
delegationScope: Routine recording may be delegated; drainage-plan changes require licensed/procedural-team direction.
examTrap: Capping a drain because output is inconvenient.
oneLinePearl: Biliary drainage changes matter most when symptoms change with them.

title: Drain Dislodgement: Do Not Push It Back In
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: A partially or completely dislodged drain can lose function, injure tissue, or contaminate the tract. Secure what remains, protect the site, and escalate—do not blindly advance the tube back into the body.
recognize: Changed external length, loosened securement, visible side holes, leakage, sudden pain, or absent drainage can signal migration.
priorities: Stop manipulation, assess the patient/site, secure the tube from further movement, and notify the procedural/surgical team.
assessMonitor: Check external length/markings, output, site bleeding/leakage, pain, vital signs, and organ-specific symptoms.
interventions: Cover an open tract/site as directed and prepare for imaging/replacement if ordered.
medicationSafety: Do not administer medications or flush through a drain whose position is uncertain.
teaching: Secure tubing during mobility and report any change in external length.
delegationScope: Dislodgement recognition/escalation requires licensed nursing action.
examTrap: Pushing the tube back to the original marking.

title: Drain Output Trends: Sudden Change Needs a Cause
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Drain output should be interpreted as a trend with the patient's symptoms and the procedure. Abrupt bleeding, foul drainage, sudden cessation, or unexpectedly increasing volume warrants reassessment rather than isolated documentation.
recognize: Different drain types have different expected outputs; the key is a meaningful change from the expected plan.
priorities: Compare current amount/color/character with prior output, site findings, pain, swelling, and vital signs.
assessMonitor: Document consistent measurement timing and characteristics and correlate with wound/organ symptoms.
interventions: Check for kinks, suction loss, dependent positioning, and securement before escalating abnormalities.
medicationSafety: Avoid empiric flushing or clamping unless the specific drain plan authorizes it.
teaching: Home patients should record trends, not just whether the bag has 'some' fluid.
delegationScope: Measurement may be delegated; clinical interpretation requires licensed judgment.
examTrap: Calling a sudden output stop 'healing' without checking the patient and device.
oneLinePearl: Every sudden drain change needs an explanation.
